column4: The rule that a person has only what they strive for makes سَعَى the precise basis of the section's labor account.
The person's striving will be seen, matching the satisfied face that turns back and sees what its effort produced.
Full recompense completes the section's sequence from intentional work through inspection to an undiminished wage.
One who wants the Hereafter and makes its due striving has effort that is thanked, directly naming successful labor and its reception.
Garden residents are told that their striving was thanked, the direct counterpart of the face pleased with its own effort.
At the overwhelming event the human remembers what they strove for, staging the retrospective inspection of labor described in the section.
Deeds are confronted and made scattered dust, a concrete realization of work whose worker receives no gain from it.
Their striving is lost in worldly life while they calculate that they work well; this joins wasted effort to a mistaken reckoning.
Works become a thirsting person's mirage; the false estimate يَحْسَبُهُ ends when God fully settles حِسَابَهُ, uniting insufficiency, miscount, and payment.
The human toils toward the Lord and will meet Him, concentrating purposeful weariness, return, and the encounter at which labor is assessed.
The right-book recipient receives an easy account, a close enactment of the reckoning that belongs to God alone.
After the easy account the recipient returns joyfully, clarifying how satisfaction follows a favorable labor account.
The other recipient calls for destruction after receiving the record behind his back; 84:10 identifies the failed side of the same account scene.
His entry into a blaze supplies the wage of the failed account begun in 84:10-11, like labor ending only in punishment.
He had calculated that he would never return, exposing the false reckoning corrected by the section's assertion that return and account are God's.
The Lord had always seen him; this explains why the mistaken confidence in 84:14 cannot remove any work from the final account.
On the day of presentation nothing about the people remains hidden, establishing the disclosure in which effort and its record are faced.
Receiving the record in the right hand identifies the speaker whose confidence about his account follows in 69:20.
The right-book recipient says he expected to meet his account, the closest parallel to a face looking back contentedly on its labor.
The resulting عِيشَةٍ رَاضِيَةٍ repeats the section's satisfaction vocabulary and locates it after a favorable account.
A high garden is the place of the pleasing life in 69:21, matching the high garden reached by the satisfied face.
Eating and drinking are explicitly granted for what was sent ahead in former days, turning sufficient garden provision into the wage of work.
Receiving the record in the left hand stages the opposite worker before his rejection of the account in 69:26.
The left-book recipient wishes he had never known his account, reversing the confident meeting of the account in 69:20.
The condemned speaker says his wealth did not avail him, using أَغْنَى in the section's sense of failing to suffice at reckoning.
Heavy scales identify the favorable measurement whose result is the pleasing life in 101:7.
The person with heavy scales enters عِيشَةٍ رَاضِيَةٍ, the same phrase that makes favorable reckoning visible as satisfaction.
Light scales stage the opposite measurement: labor enters the account but lacks the weight needed for a satisfying return.
The abyss is the destination produced by the light scales in 101:8, completing the failed side of the wage scene.
God says every thing has been enumerated in a record, a literal counterpart to the section's definition of account as counting things one by one.
No vain speech or lie is heard in the garden, directly paralleling the garden from which لَاغِيَة is absent.
The righteous receive recompense as عَطَاءً حِسَابًا, the sufficient gift that answers labor whose provision did not suffice.
Thirst, hunger, and نَصَب in God's path are written as a righteous deed and earn an undiminished wage, reversing toil that yields only toil.
They have a نَصِيب from what they earned and God is swift in account, joining the section's audible sense of share to acquisition and reckoning.
Men and women each have a نَصِيب of what they earn, stating directly that purposeful acquisition produces an apportioned share.
God will pay each group its نَصِيب without diminution, turning the secondary share sense beside نَاصِبَة into exact settlement.
The seeker of the worldly harvest receives some of it but has no afterlife share, while the afterlife harvest is increased; aim determines labor's return.
Just scales omit nothing even as small as a mustard seed, and كَفَىٰ بِنَا حَاسِبِينَ joins exact reckoning to divine sufficiency.
The record leaves neither small nor great without counting it and people find their deeds present, concretely staging the section's enumeration.
God does not take people to account for لَغْو in oaths but does for what hearts earn, exactly joining excluded speech to accountable acquisition.
Laghw in oaths is not taken to account, whereas deliberately bound oaths are; this supplies the section's boundary between surplus and countable intent.
Garden provision is recompense for what its people used to do; 56:25 then specifies that vain speech is absent from that earned setting.
Garden residents hear neither لَغْوًا nor sinful speech, a direct lexical and scenic parallel to the section's silent garden.
Peace is the only speech heard, positively completing the absence of vain speech stated in 56:25.
The garden cup contains neither لَغْو nor sin, placing the same excluded speech amid the rewarded hospitality described by the section.
Garden inhabitants hear no لَغْو, only peace, while their provision arrives continually; absence of emptiness accompanies sufficient provision.
When believers hear لَغْو they turn away and distinguish “our deeds” from “your deeds,” tightly linking discarded speech with separate labor accounts.
The soul returns رَاضِيَةً مَرْضِيَّةً, expressing in one line both the servant's satisfaction and God's satisfaction named in the section.
The mutually satisfied soul of 89:28 enters God's garden, completing the same movement from accepted labor to a satisfying garden.
Everlasting gardens are the reward where God is pleased with them and they with Him, explicitly realizing both directions of رضا.
For the truthful, gardens and mutual satisfaction—رَضِىَ ٱللَّهُ عَنْهُمْ وَرَضُوا۟ عَنْهُ—form the profitable outcome of the day of accounting.
God's pleasure with the faithful and theirs with Him is followed by prepared gardens, again tying reciprocal رضا to final reward.
God is pleased with a faithful people and they with Him, then admits them to gardens; divine approval and human contentment meet in the wage.
“Your striving is diverse” makes labor the fork from which the surah's opposed outcomes of ease and hardship proceed.
The miser's wealth will not avail him when he falls, using يُغْنِى in the same failed-sufficiency sense as the useless food.
After giving for God's approval, the person “will surely be satisfied,” making رضا the end of a correctly directed striving.
The Hour is coming so that every soul may be recompensed for what it strives for, an exact statement of effort entering God's account.
The command to work is followed by God seeing the work and by return to the Knower, who discloses what was done.
People emerge separately to be shown their deeds, establishing the display whose smallest entries 99:7-8 then specify.
An atom's weight of good is seen, matching the section's claim that labor itself will be looked upon and counted.
An atom's weight of evil is likewise seen, preventing failed effort from disappearing outside the account.
God has enumerated deeds that their doers forgot, sharply distinguishing divine counting from the worker's incomplete memory.
God's record speaks truth because what people did was copied, giving the labor account a concrete written form.
God writes what people sent ahead and their traces and enumerates everything in a clear register, a direct image of comprehensive counting.
Everything people did is in the records, locating intentional acts inside the final inventory.
Every small and great matter is inscribed, specifying the exhaustive scale of the deed records named in 54:52.
Every soul finds the good and evil it did present, matching the face that turns and sees what its labor has become.
The human is informed of what was sent ahead and left behind, making the final account include the full temporal reach of action.
Honored guardians are recording scribes; 82:12 identifies deeds as the material they know.
The recorders know whatever people do, directly supplying the inventory behind the final reckoning.
The weighing that day is true, and heavy scales yield success; labor's value is measured rather than merely asserted.
Light scales identify those who lost themselves through wrongdoing, the failed side of measured labor.
Those whose scales are heavy prosper, a direct parallel to effort whose final weight satisfies its owner.
Those whose scales are light lose themselves and remain in Hell, making deficient labor produce the opposite wage.
Fire scorches their faces after the light-scale verdict in 23:103, returning the failed reckoning visibly to the face.
A good deed receives tenfold while an evil deed receives only its like, specifying the just rates in the labor account.
God does not wrong even an atom's weight and multiplies good, joining microscopic accounting to generous payment.
A greeting must be repaid better or equally, and God is حَسِيبًا over everything; measured reciprocation and reckoning occur together.
God repays those who do evil for what they did and those who do good with the best, stating the two wages of action.
Each soul is recompensed for what it earned without wrong, a compact formulation of labor, settlement, and exact justice.
People have ranks according to their deeds so that God may pay their works in full, turning qualitative labor into an undiminished allocation.
After all are returned to God, each soul is fully paid what it earned, matching the section's sequence of return followed by account.
When gathered for the certain day, each soul is paid in full for what it earned; gathering makes the wage universal and exact.
Every soul receives its wages in full on Resurrection Day, explicitly locating complete payment after mortal labor.
On the day each soul pleads for itself, it is fully paid for what it did without wrong, an individualized work account.
Every soul is paid in full for what it did, and God best knows their deeds; complete knowledge grounds complete settlement.
Every soul is recompensed for what it earned with no injustice and a swift account, directly combining acquisition, wage, and reckoning.
God repays each soul for what it earned and is swift in account, making earned outcome the express purpose of the final scene.
Those who believe and do righteous deeds receive their wages in full, directly realizing the dictionary link between intentional work and pay.
Believing workers are paid their wages fully and receive additional bounty, showing the wage can exceed the deed without omitting it.
God says He does not waste the wage of anyone who does good work, the positive boundary against labor yielding only fatigue.
Reciters, prayer, and giving form a trade that does not fail because God pays their wages fully and adds bounty.
Forgiveness and gardens are called an excellent wage for workers, directly pairing عَامِلِين with أَجْر.
Believing workers are lodged in high garden chambers, followed by “excellent is the wage of workers,” a close labor-to-height correspondence.
Garden inheritors praise the fulfilled promise and the verse concludes “excellent is the wage of workers,” naming the garden as earned pay.
After the garden victory, “for the like of this let the workers work” makes that result the proper object of purposeful labor.
What humans possess runs out while what is with God remains, and patient people are paid by their best deeds; enduring wage answers expended labor.
Righteous work receives a good life and a reward based on the best deeds, directly linking labor, pleasing life, and payment.
No soul knows the comfort hidden for them as recompense for what they did, showing a wage whose sufficiency surpasses the worker's present sight.
Righteous workers enter the garden and are provided for بِغَيْرِ حِسَابٍ, contrasting exact deed reckoning with reward beyond measure.
The patient are paid their wage without measure, a concrete boundary to “account” as finite enumeration.
Garden residents are told to eat and drink pleasantly for what they used to do, making satisfying food the direct pay of action.
The righteous eat and drink pleasantly for what they used to do, reversing food that cannot satisfy hunger.
God says this is how doers of good are recompensed, explicitly interpreting the sufficient provision of 77:43 as their wage.
The garden is inherited because of what its people used to do, identifying the lasting habitation as labor's return.
Garden heirs say they could not have reached it without God's guidance, while the call states they inherited it for their deeds.
Those wanting worldly life receive the full return of their deeds there; 11:16 reveals that this exhausts their wage before the Hereafter.
For worldly workers only the Fire remains, and what they made is void, the clearest parallel to labor whose sole gain is weariness.
Disbelievers' deeds are ashes scattered by a violent wind and they can gain nothing from what they earned, a vivid image of unusable labor.
A showy charity becomes dust washed from bare rock, leaving its giver unable to gain anything earned; effort and expected wage vanish together.
The question about the greatest losers in deeds introduces the people whose miscalculated striving is specified in 18:104.
Their works collapse and receive no weight on Resurrection Day, completing the lost striving and wrong calculation of 18:104.
Believing workers receive gardens as hospitality, supplying the deliberate opposite outcome to the lost workers of 18:103-105.
Those who disbelieve and block God's way have their deeds led astray, describing purposeful activity deprived of its intended return.
Believers who do righteous work have their evils removed and their state repaired, the paired successful side of the failed deeds in 47:1.
Neither wealth nor what the condemned man earned avails him, joining failed sufficiency to acquisition in a single line.
What earlier rejecters earned did not avail them, making acquisition itself incapable of becoming sufficient protection.
The evils they earned then struck them, supplying the actual wage after 39:50 denies that their gains could avail.
Past peoples' abundant acquisitions did not avail them, another direct use of earning followed by failed sufficiency.
Neither what they earned nor their protectors avail them before Hell, uniting useless gain, failed sufficiency, and punishment.
On the final day wealth and children do not avail, setting a sharp limit on what can count as sufficient capital.
Only one who comes with a sound heart escapes the insufficiency named in 26:88, identifying what remains valid at the account.
The messenger's duty is only delivery while “upon Us is the account,” almost exactly restating the section's division of roles.
Noah says his followers' account rests only with his Lord, the same boundary that reserves final counting to God.
The Prophet bears none of the believers' account and they bear none of his, guarding the divine ownership of reckoning.
The God-fearing bear none of the mockers' account but must remind them, joining the section's reminder stance to separated liability.
People are returned to God, their true Master, to whom judgment belongs and who is swiftest in account; return and counting meet explicitly.
Every soul is held in pledge for what it earned, making acquisition an inescapably personal liability.
Each person is a pledge for what they earned even when believing families are reunited, preserving the individual labor account.
Evildoers wrongly calculate that they will be made equal to believing righteous workers; the verse rejects an undifferentiated wage.
God asks whether righteous workers could be treated like corrupters, defining fair reckoning through the required distinction between their labors.
Life and death are created to test who is best in deed, making purposeful work the object of divine assessment.
Garden inhabitants say no نَصَب or weariness touches them there, the exact reversal of a face whose labor remains upon it as exhaustion.
No نَصَب touches garden inhabitants and they never leave, opposing both fruitless fatigue and the instability of a merely worldly gain.
Adam is warned that expulsion from the garden would make him toil, locating weariness outside the garden where the satisfied face rests.
Inside the garden Adam neither hungers nor lacks clothing, the direct positive boundary to food that does not avail against hunger.
The garden also removes thirst and exposure to heat, completing the sufficient provision opposed to punishment's useless food and drink.
The righteous feed others while seeking neither human recompense nor thanks, qualifying the section's wage principle: their intended pay is from God.
The giver acts without any person's favor needing repayment, excluding social exchange from the labor account that ends in satisfaction.
The giver seeks only the face of the Most High, fixing the aim that makes the satisfaction promised in 92:21 a divine wage.
God alone enriches and grants sufficiency, setting the source of genuine غِنَى against food, wealth, and earnings that fail to avail.
Human transgression begins when a person treats himself as independent, introducing the false sufficiency named in 96:7.
Seeing oneself as ٱسْتَغْنَى is the opposite of recognizing that created gains cannot suffice at the final account.
The return is to the Lord despite the person's claim of self-sufficiency, correcting that claim through the same return-account sequence as the section.
Rejecters command one another to make noise, وَٱلْغَوْا, during the Quran; their manufactured babble contrasts with the garden where no vain speech is heard.
There is no blame for an honest mistake, only for what hearts intend, defining the purposeful boundary that makes an act accountable work.
No utterance escapes an observing recorder; alongside the oath exceptions in 2:225 and 5:89, this distinguishes recording speech from liability for laghw.
God feeds Quraysh against hunger, a compact image of provision that truly suffices where the punishment food cannot.
Humans cannot enumerate God's favors, reversing the direction of the section's final count: divine gifts exceed human counting while God counts people.
God gives from what people ask, yet they cannot enumerate His favors; abundance outruns the creature's حساب while creaturely deeds remain accountable.
A good intercession yields a نَصِيب from it and an evil one a corresponding burden, extending the share sense to a deliberate intervention's return.
Guardians must hand over orphan property after assessment and keep no wasteful wage, with God sufficient as حَسِيبًا; stewardship becomes literal reckoning.
Whoever relies on God finds that He is حَسْبُهُ, using the account root's sufficiency branch to locate enoughness in the giver rather than the wage.
Worldly life deceives rejecters while believers stand above them at Resurrection and God provides without account, linking final rank to unmeasured provision.
Believers turn away from لَغْو in worldly life; their deliberate refusal anticipates the garden where such speech is not heard at all.
God's servants pass by لَغْو with dignity, a lived counterpart to the final environment from which vain speech has disappeared.
The person who turns away strives to corrupt the earth and destroy crops and offspring, giving concrete form to the dictionary claim that سَعْي can be evil work.
Striving to ruin places where God is remembered supplies another morally failed سَعْي whose object determines its eventual account.
Those who strive to frustrate God's signs are assigned the Blaze, explicitly giving hostile striving its corresponding wage.
Those who strive against God's signs receive painful punishment, a repeated negative instance of effort measured by its aim.
Striving to defeat God's signs ends with the strivers brought into punishment, making failed hostile effort visible at its destination.
Job names his affliction as نُصْب and torment, confirming the fatigue sense heard in the worked and weary face without itself supplying a wage scene.
Moses' companion says their journey has brought نَصَب, a concrete instance of purposeful movement leaving fatigue on the traveler.
The command فَٱنصَبْ after finishing directs renewed exertion toward the Lord, setting purposeful fatigue on the successful side of labor.
Humanity is created in toil, broadening the worked face's exhaustion into the ordinary condition from which the final wage acquires urgency.
The Lord will give until the addressee is satisfied, pairing divine gift with رضا even though the verse does not itself name the preceding work.
Monasticism is invented seeking God's pleasure but not duly observed; believers among them receive wages, bringing intention, failed performance, رضا, and pay together.
God is pleased with gratitude while every soul bears only its own burden, linking divine رضا to individualized responsibility.
A voluntary good act finds God appreciative and knowing, a close nonlexical parallel to striving that is “thanked.”
Whoever earns a good deed receives increase in it and God is appreciative, explaining how a worker's gain can be acknowledged beyond bare equivalence.
The closing question asks whether disbelievers have been repaid for what they used to do, presenting final recompense as the verdict on their conduct.
Whoever hopes to meet the Lord must do righteous work sincerely, joining purposeful action to the encounter where the account occurs.
The human wrongly calculates that he will be left aimless, a mistaken حساب-like assumption that would erase purposeful work and final settlement.
God asks whether people calculated that they were created pointlessly and would not return, directly opposing the denial of return and account.
Feeding the needy, orphan, and captive is the concrete deed whose disavowal of human payment follows in 76:9 and whose divine wage appears in 76:12 and 76:22.
God recompenses their patience with a garden and silk, explicitly making the garden hospitality that culminates in 76:22 a wage.
Silver vessels and cups circulate among the garden people, supplying the particular hospitality immediately before their striving is pronounced thanked in 76:22.
The silver vessels are precisely measured, adding measured provision to the garden scene whose guests' effort receives acknowledgment in 76:22.
The Lord clothes the garden people and gives them a pure drink; this is the last concrete gift before 76:22 identifies the whole reception as their wage.
One who wants the immediate life receives only the allotted portion God wills and then Hell, the deliberately failed counterpart to the afterlife striving in 17:19.
The great overwhelming event arrives, naming the event at which 79:35 says each person remembers their striving.
Hell is exposed to everyone who can see immediately after remembered striving, turning the review of work into a visible outcome.
The transgressor opens the failed branch of the reckoning that follows the recollection of striving in 79:35.
Preferring the nearer life identifies the aim of the failed worker whose destination 79:39 states.
Hell is the abode of the one who preferred worldly life, completing the negative wage of 79:37-38.
Fearing the Lord's station and restraining desire identify the contrary labor whose destination follows in 79:41.
The garden is the abode of the self-restraining person, completing the successful wage after striving is remembered.
No bearer bears another's burden; just before the rule about striving, this makes each labor account personally nontransferable.
The final destination is to the Lord, completing the effort-and-recompense sequence of 53:39-41 with the owner of the account.
Hell is named as the recompense of those whose striving was lost and whose deeds had no weight in 18:104-105.
A fiercely hot fire identifies the abyss reached by the person with light scales, completing that failed account's destination.
Giving and guarding oneself begin the successful form of the diverse striving announced in 92:4.
Affirming the best promise supplies the conviction that directs the giver's effort toward its favorable result.
God eases the giver toward ease, making rightly aimed striving issue in a fitting path and outcome.
Withholding and deeming oneself self-sufficient, ٱسْتَغْنَىٰ, begin the failed branch of striving and expose false sufficiency as its motive.
Denying the best promise supplies the orientation that makes the miser's effort fail.
God eases the miser toward hardship, giving the second form of diverse striving its contrary result.
Each person's record is fastened to them and brought out as an open book, concretely attaching the account to its worker.
The person is told to read their own record and is sufficient that day as an accountant against themself, joining self-inspection, sufficiency, and reckoning.
Receiving the book in the right hand identifies the favorable account holder before 84:8 states that his reckoning is easy.
Receiving the book behind the back identifies the failed account holder before his call for destruction in 84:11.
His former joy among his family contrasts with the lasting joy after an easy account and explains the false expectation of no return in 84:14.
Everyone has ranks according to what they did, so differing labor receives a differentiated outcome under God's complete awareness.
No deed escapes God's witness, not even an atom's weight, and everything is in a clear record; this is exhaustive labor accounting.
God has encompassed people and counted them exactly, a direct formulation of the section's counting sense of account.
Each person comes to God individually, showing the personal presentation produced by the exact count in 19:94.
Even a mustard-seed weight hidden in rock, heaven, or earth is brought by God, showing that no minute work can escape the account.
Not an atom's weight or anything smaller or greater escapes God; all is in a clear record, specifying the precision of final counting.
A record speaks truth and no one is wronged, while obligation stays within capacity; the account measures real work without manufacturing impossible liability.
Every expenditure and journey is written as a righteous deed so God may reward the best of their work, continuing 9:120's accounting of fatigue itself.
Those in lasting punishment are asked whether they are being recompensed for anything but what they earned, identifying torment as settled acquisition.
Faces are cast into the fire and asked whether they are repaid except for what they did, visibly joining deed, wage, and punished face.
On that day no soul is wronged and people are recompensed only for what they did, stating the exact labor settlement.
The condemned are recompensed only for what they used to do, defining punishment as the corresponding wage of action.
Disbelievers are told not to excuse themselves that day because they are repaid only for what they did, making the account answer deed rather than plea.
Righteous work benefits its doer and evil works against its doer, while the Lord wrongs no servant; action returns to its source justly.
Whoever works righteousness does so for themself and whoever does evil works against themself, before all return to the Lord.
Doing good benefits the doer and doing evil harms the doer, expressing the return of labor upon its worker.
Every soul earns only against itself and no bearer carries another's burden before return to God, defining the account's personal ownership.
Each soul receives the good it earns and bears the evil it earns, a compact two-sided ledger of acquisition.
On Resurrection Day every soul is fully paid what it earned without wrong, another exact formulation of completed wages.
Whoever does evil is recompensed for it and finds no protector against God, preventing harmful work from escaping settlement.
Believing righteous workers enter the garden without even a speck of wrong, supplying the favorable side of 4:123's deed account.
The Lord will fully repay everyone for their deeds and is informed of what they do, joining complete knowledge to full payment.
Whatever good people spend is fully repaid to them without wrong, making voluntary expenditure an action with an exact return.
Whatever is spent in God's path is fully repaid without injustice, another explicit conversion of purposeful outlay into undiminished wage.
Those who deny God's signs have their works nullified and are asked whether they are recompensed except for what they did.
Those who turn back from faith lose their deeds in both worlds and remain in the Fire, making sustained work end without profitable share.
Their works fail in this world and the Hereafter and no helpers remain, a repeated formulation of labor stripped of every return.
Rejecting faith makes work collapse and leaves the person among afterlife losers, linking null labor to final loss.
The idolaters' works collapse and they remain in the Fire, a direct pairing of wasted activity with its failed wage.
They enjoyed their allotted share as earlier peoples did, but their works collapsed; temporary portion and final loss meet in one reckoning.
Because they hated what God sent down, He made their works collapse; rejection removes the hoped-for return of labor.
Following what angers God and disliking His pleasure causes works to collapse, tying divine رضا and the survival of deeds together.
Their spending resembles a freezing wind that destroys a wrongdoer's crop, a concrete agricultural image of expended labor losing its yield.
A treasured garden burns when its owner is old and dependents are weak, dramatizing the ruin of an expected yield precisely when its wage is needed.
The faithful rejoice that God does not waste the believers' wage, directly affirming preservation of earned return.
Those who hold to the Book and establish prayer learn that God does not waste the wage of reformers.
Patience is commanded because God does not waste the wage of doers of good, setting endurance against fruitless weariness.
Joseph is established in the land and the verse states that God does not waste the wage of doers of good, showing preserved labor in worldly placement.
Joseph says that reverence and patience are not lost because God does not waste the wage of doers of good, explaining his satisfaction after long trial.
God asks whether those who submit could be made like criminals, rejecting a reckoning that gives opposed workers the same wage.
“What is wrong with you; how do you judge?” exposes the faulty calculation behind the impossible equality posed in 68:35.
Solomon is told that God's gift may be bestowed or withheld without account, placing sovereign abundance beyond the finite counting applied to human work.
The hoarder calculates that wealth has made him immortal; the following fire corrects a false estimate of wealth's sufficiency and lasting wage.
God extends His gift to both the immediate-life seeker and the afterlife striver, clarifying that present provision alone is not the final labor verdict.
Worldly preferences differ, but the Hereafter has greater ranks and preference; this explains the larger return of the striving in 17:19.
The verse points to what is in Moses' scrolls, locating the labor-account rule of 53:39 in the source tradition named by the section.
Abraham who fulfilled is named beside Moses, completing the scriptural attribution that frames the rules in 53:38-41.
God says guidance rests upon Him in the same passage that separates diverse strivings and their outcomes.
The first life and the Hereafter belong to God, grounding His authority over both the labor period and its final wage.
God says He is counting for the rejecters a count, a non-ḥisāb formulation of the deliberate divine enumeration developed in the section.
God encompasses what His messengers carry and counts everything numerically, extending divine counting to exhaustive knowledge.
Seeking God's pleasure is set against incurring His wrath, so رضا marks a decisive difference in the final valuation of action.
The two groups have differing degrees with God, giving the opposed relation to divine pleasure in 3:162 a measured outcome.
Gardens and lasting dwellings are promised, but God's pleasure is declared greater, ranking رضا above even the visible wage.
God is pleased with the believers' pledged intention and rewards them with a near victory, a historical instance of divine رضا becoming recompense.
The faithful seek bounty and divine pleasure, and righteous workers among them are promised forgiveness and a great wage.
The question whether believers calculate they will enter the garden before severe trial challenges an account that expects reward without tested effort.
The question whether people calculate they will enter the garden before their striving and patience are disclosed links hoped-for reward to proven labor.
